description: Bizim yapmamız gereken; 7-12 yaş arası çocukların bir ay veya Mars üssünü yönetmelerini, yaşam desteği, radyasyon kalkanı, enerji bütçesi, gıda üretimi ve iletişim gecikmesi hakkında gerçekçi kararlar almalarını ve bu seçimlerin simüle edilmiş bir görev boyunca nasıl sonuçlandığını deneyimlemelerini sağlayan etkileşimli bir oyun veya uygulama tasarlamak ve geliştirmektir.
summary: MARS: Colony Builder is a free, browser-based 3D survival game that turns real NASA science into gameplay. Players fly by rocket from an Earth base to Mars, gather resources, build and upgrade a colony, and survive hazards modeled on actual mission data. Radiation doses come from Curiosity’s RAD measurements and are tracked against NASA’s 600 mSv career limit, while dust storms, solar particle events and marsquakes test the player’s planning. Farming uses 11 crops really grown on the ISS and in Mars soil experiments, with growth times based on real days to harvest; a soil analyzer shows fertility, pH, perchlorate and water from Phoenix and Curiosity data. Messages from Houston arrive with true light delay through the Deep Space Network, accompanied by real NASA audio. A story mode, three difficulty levels, an engine-repair mini game and a context-aware in-game guide make the science easy to follow. The game runs from a single HTML file with raw WebGL, needs no installation, supports up to four players with voice radio, and is available in five languages. Our goal is to help students understand what living on Mars would really demand, by learning through play instead of memorization.
details:
What exactly does the project do?
MARS: Colony Builder is a browser game where the player flies by rocket from a base on Earth to Mars, gathers resources, builds a colony, grows crops and brings samples back to Earth for analysis. Along the way the player faces real mission hazards: solar radiation storms, dust storms, marsquakes and engine failures.

How does it work?
The whole game is a single HTML file that opens in any modern browser with no installation. The 3D world is drawn with WebGL, and every frame the game updates time, health, radiation, crop growth and messages from Earth. Real NASA numbers drive these systems. For example, the player receives 0.64 mSv of radiation per day on Mars, as measured by Curiosity, and must hide in a shelter when a solar storm warning arrives. The soil meter shows pH, perchlorate and nitrate values within the ranges measured by Phoenix and Curiosity. Crops such as radish (27 days) and dwarf wheat (70 days) grow on the real timescales of NASA’s ISS experiments. Messages from Houston arrive through the Deep Space Network with a light delay. In multiplayer, a small Node.js server connects up to 4 players, who talk over a voice radio built with WebRTC.

What problem does it aim to solve?
The real challenges of a Mars mission are explained mostly in technical papers, so students rarely learn them in a memorable way.

What benefits does it bring to users and society?
Students learn science by making decisions instead of memorising facts. Teachers get a free classroom tool that runs on school computers and phones. Five languages (Turkish, English, Spanish, Korean, German) make it usable in many countries, and the open-source code lets others build on it.

What outcome do you want to achieve?
We want young people to understand why radiation, soil chemistry and communication delays matter for Mars exploration, and to become curious about space science. Our next steps are a pilot in schools, a shared colony for multiplayer and Martian seasons; these are not built yet.

Which programming languages, hardware, tools and technologies did you use?
Languages: JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3 and GLSL. Technologies: WebGL for 3D graphics, Web Audio API for sound, WebRTC and Server-Sent Events for multiplayer, Node.js for the server, and browser storage for saving. Testing: automated browser tests with Playwright. Hardware: none required, any computer, tablet or phone with a browser. No game engine or external library was used.
